brain.def: The organ inside the skull that, with the spinal cord, makes up the central nervous system; it controls the body and produces thought, emotion and behavior.

brainstem.def: The oldest part of the brain, joining the spinal cord to the rest of the brain; it controls automatic survival functions and contains the medulla and the reticular activating system.

medulla.def: The base of the brainstem, which controls heart rate and breathing.

reticular.def: A network of neurons running through the brainstem that controls arousal: waking, sleeping, alertness and attention to the surroundings.

reward-center.def: A set of structures deep in the brain, including the nucleus accumbens, where dopamine signals produce pleasure and drive motivation toward rewards such as food and, in addiction, drugs.

cerebellum.def: The "little brain" at the back, under the cerebrum, that coordinates balance and smooth, timed movement and helps with some kinds of learning.

cerebral-cortex.def: The thin, wrinkled outer layer of the brain's two hemispheres, where sensing, planning, language and thinking take place.

hemisphere.def: One of the two halves of the cerebrum, left and right, joined by the corpus callosum.

frontal-lobe.def: The lobe at the front of each hemisphere, involved in planning, judgment, decision making and movement; it contains the motor cortex and Broca's area.

prefrontal.def: The front part of the frontal lobe, involved in planning, judgment, impulse control and personality.

motor-cortex.def: A strip at the back of the frontal lobe that sends commands for voluntary movement to muscles on the opposite side of the body.

parietal-lobe.def: The lobe at the top and upper back of each hemisphere that processes touch and body position and helps with spatial reasoning.

somatosensory.def: A strip at the front of the parietal lobe, just behind the motor cortex, that registers touch, temperature and pain from the opposite side of the body.

occipital-lobe.def: The lobe at the back of each hemisphere that processes visual information.

temporal-lobe.def: The lobe on the side of each hemisphere, below the lateral fissure, that processes hearing and contains Wernicke's area.

association-areas.def: Areas of the cortex not tied to one sense or movement that combine information for higher thinking such as learning, remembering, judging and speaking.

limbic-system.def: A group of structures deep in the brain, below the cortex, involved in emotion, drives and memory, including the hippocampus and amygdala.

thalamus.def: The brain's sensory relay station: it routes signals from every sense except smell to the right areas of the cortex.

hypothalamus.def: A small structure below the thalamus that keeps homeostasis by regulating hunger, thirst, body temperature and sex drive, and directs the pituitary gland.

homeostasis.def: The body's tendency to keep a steady internal state, such as body temperature and blood sugar, by correcting changes.

hippocampus.def: A curved structure deep in each temporal lobe that is needed to form new memories of facts and events.

amygdala.def: Two almond-shaped clusters deep in the temporal lobes involved in fear and other emotional reactions to threats.

corpus-callosum.def: The thick band of axons that connects the left and right hemispheres and lets them share information.

contralateral.def: The crossed wiring of the brain: each hemisphere receives sensations from, and controls movement on, the opposite side of the body.

lateralization.def: The tendency of each hemisphere to be more involved in certain tasks, such as language mostly on the left in most people; the two still work together.

split-brain.def: A condition in which the corpus callosum has been cut, usually to treat severe epilepsy, so the two hemispheres cannot share information directly.

brocas-area.def: An area in the lower left frontal lobe in most people that helps produce speech; damage makes speech slow and effortful.

wernickes-area.def: An area in the upper back of the left temporal lobe in most people that helps understand language; damage leaves speech fluent but hard to understand.

aphasia.def: Loss of the ability to produce or understand language after brain damage, such as Broca's aphasia (slow, effortful speech) or Wernicke's aphasia (fluent speech with little meaning).

plasticity.def: The brain's ability to change by forming new connections and reorganizing after learning or damage; it is greatest in childhood.

eeg.def: Electroencephalogram: a recording of the brain's electrical activity from electrodes on the scalp; it shows when activity changes, millisecond by millisecond, but not precisely where.

fmri.def: Functional magnetic resonance imaging: a scan that tracks blood oxygen changes to show which brain areas are more active during a task; good for where, slower for when.

lesion.def: Damaged or destroyed brain tissue, from injury or disease, or made on purpose in animal research to learn what a region does.
